title: Sir Philip Sidney's Cup of Water
text:
Sir Philip Sidney was the model of the English gentleman of his age: poet, courtier, diplomat and soldier. In 1586 he was serving with the English army helping the Dutch against Spain. On September 22, at a skirmish outside Zutphen, he rode into action without his thigh armor and was struck by a musket ball above the knee.

His friend and biographer Fulke Greville tells what happened as he was carried back from the field, thirsty from loss of blood. Someone brought him a bottle of drink, traditionally remembered as water. As he raised it to his mouth he saw a dying foot soldier being carried past, who looked longingly at it. Sidney handed the water to the man before drinking any himself, saying, "Thy necessity is yet greater than mine."

The wound became infected, and Sidney died at Arnhem about three weeks later, at the age of thirty one. England gave him a grand state funeral in London, and the story of the water became one of the best remembered acts of chivalry in English history.
lesson: Real kindness sometimes means giving up what you badly need to someone whose need is greater. It is noticed most when it costs the most.
source: Fulke Greville, The Life of the Renowned Sir Philip Sidney (written c. 1610, published 1652)
caveat: The story comes only from Greville, writing about twenty five years later, and cannot be confirmed by other witnesses.
